Dataset title: Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES)
Description: The Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES) replaced and integrated seven annual business surveys (Annual Retail Trade Survey, Annual Wholesale Survey, Service Annual Survey, Annual Survey of Manufactures, Annual Capital Expenditures Survey, Manufacturer's Unfilled Orders Survey , Report of Organization) into one survey. The AIES provides the most comprehensive national and subnational data on business revenues, expenses, payroll, and employment on an annual basis.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

Census Bureau


Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for Review and Approval; Comment 
Request; Annual Integrated Economic Survey

    The Department of Commerce will submit the following information 
collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for 
review and clearance in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 
1995, on or after the date of publication of this notice. We invite the 
general public and other Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and 
continuing information collections, which helps us assess the impact of 
our information collection requirements and minimize the public's 
reporting burden. Public comments were previously requested via the 
Federal Register on November 21, 2022 during a 60-day comment period. 
This notice allows for an additional 30 days for public comments.
    Agency: U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce.
    Title: Annual Integrated Economic Survey.
    OMB Control Number: None.
    Form Number(s): This electronic collection has no form number.
    Type of Request: Regular submission, New Information Collection 
Request.
    Number of Respondents: Dress Rehearsal--8,470 and 50 debriefing 
interviews; Full AIES--384,940.
    Average Hours per Response: Dress Rehearsal--3 hours and 55 
minutes, Debriefing interviews--1 hour; Full AIES--3 hours and 23 
minutes.
    Burden Hours: Dress Rehearsal--33,206 hours, Debriefing 
interviews--50 hours; Full AIES--1,300,535 hours.
    Needs and Uses: The U.S. Census Bureau requests Office of 
Management and Budget (OMB) approval to conduct the Annual Integrated 
Economic Survey (AIES) on an annual basis, beginning for survey year 
2023 (collected in calendar year 2024) and a preparatory Dress 
Rehearsal for the AIES for survey year 2022 (collected in calendar year 
2023). The AIES is a new survey designed to integrate and replace seven 
existing annual business surveys into one survey. The AIES will provide 
the only comprehensive national and subnational data on business 
revenues, expenses, and assets on an annual basis. The AIES is designed 
to combine Census Bureau collections to reduce respondent burden, 
increase data quality, and allow the Census Bureau to operate more 
efficiently to reduce long term costs. The existing collections 
integrated into the AIES are the Annual Retail Trade Survey (ARTS), 
Annual Wholesale Trade Survey (AWTS), Service Annual Survey (SAS), 
Annual Survey of Manufactures (ASM), Annual Capital Expenditures Survey 
(ACES), Manufacturers' Unfilled Orders Survey (M3UFO), and the Report 
of Organization.
    The AIES will collect the following information from employer 
businesses in sample:

 Business characteristics, including employment, operating 
status, organizational change, ownership information, and co-op status
 Business classification, including business activity, type of 
operation, and tax status
 Revenue, including sales, shipments, and receipts, revenue by 
class of customer, taxes, contributions, gifts, and grants, products, 
and e-commerce activity
 Operating expenses, including purchased services, payroll, 
benefits, rental payments, utilities, interest, resales, equipment, 
materials and supplies, research and development, and other detailed 
operating expenses
 Assets, including capital expenditures, inventories, and 
depreciable assets
 Robotic equipment

    Additional topics of collections in the AIES include sources of 
revenue and/or expense for providers (e.g., hospitals and other 
businesses in the health industry) of select services such as inpatient 
days, outpatient visits to hospitals, patient visits for other selected 
health industries, revenue from telemedicine services, and expenses for 
electronic health records. Product data will be collected from 
businesses operating in manufacturing industries. Merchandise lines 
data will be collected from businesses operating in select retail 
industries. Detailed inventories will be collected for trucks, truck 
tractors, and trailers.
    The AIES may include new questions each year based on relevant 
business topics. Potential topics for such new questions could include 
technological advances, management and business practices, exporting 
practices, and globalization. Any new questions will be submitted to 
OMB for review using the appropriate clearance vehicle.
    Beginning in August of 2023, the Census Bureau plans to conduct a 
Dress Rehearsal for the AIES with approximately 8,470 companies. The 
Dress Rehearsal will collect survey year 2022 information. The Dress 
Rehearsal will be a large-scale test of the forms and procedures 
planned for the AIES. The burden estimate is 3 hours and 55 minutes per 
respondent. The Dress rehearsal will allow us to examine patterns of 
non-response and to determine what additional support respondents will 
need. Paradata gathered from respondents' interactions with the online 
collection instrument during the Dress Rehearsal will help refine our 
burden estimate. We will also compare the quality of responses received 
to historical data collected in the 7 surveys the AIES will replace. Up 
to 50, 1-hour debriefing interviews with respondents will also be 
conducted.
    To minimize the burden imposed on most respondents already in 
sample for the seven annual surveys the AIES will replace, we will use 
the AIES responses from companies that participate in the Dress 
Rehearsal to satisfy their reporting requirement for the annual 
survey(s) for which they are in sample for the 2022 survey year. Given 
that the AIES Dress Rehearsal will be conducted during the same 
calendar year as we will be conducting the 2022 Economic Census, we may 
use the AIES Dress Rehearsal to supplement Economic Census responses, 
pursuant to title 13 U.S.C. 193.
    After conclusion of the Dress Rehearsal, and based on refinements 
made to forms and procedures, the Census Bureau will begin conducting 
the full-scale AIES in 2024, collecting survey year 2023 information. 
The AIES will select a stratified sequential random sample of 
approximately 384,940 companies from a frame of approximately 5.4 
million companies

[[Page 19907]]

constructed from the BR, which is the Census Bureau's master business 
list.
    The AIES covers domestic, nonfarm employer businesses with 
operations during the survey year. Non-employer businesses are not 
within the scope of this new AIES. The Census Bureau will submit a 
separate request for approval to collect data from non-employer 
businesses, if it is determined that a collection is needed to produce 
those estimates. Businesses which reported business activity on 
Internal Revenue Service (IRS) tax forms 941, ``Employer's Quarterly 
Federal Tax Return''; 944, ``Employer's Annual Federal Tax Return''; 
1065 ``U.S. Return of Partnership Income''; or any one of the 1120 
corporate tax forms will be eligible for selection.

their requirement to respond and how to access the survey. Responses 
will be due approximately 30 days from receipt. Select businesses will 
receive a due date reminder via a letter or email prior to the due 
date. Additionally, email follow-ups and up to three mail follow-ups to 
nonrespondents will be conducted at approximately one-month intervals. 
Selected nonrespondents will receive a priority class mailing for the 
third follow-up if needed. Selected nonrespondents will also receive 
follow-up telephone calls.
    The AIES will replace the ARTS, AWTS, SAS, ASM, ACES, M3UFO, and 
the Report of Organization for survey year 2023, at which time the 
Census Bureau will officially sunset these programs. The ASM and the 
Report of Organization completed their final year of data collection in 
survey year 2021. ACES, ARTS, AWTS, SAS, and M3UFO will complete their 
final year of data collection in survey year 2022.
    The Census Bureau will submit a revision request to OMB prior to 
conducting the full-scale AIES to finalize any details presented in 
this request that may change.
    Estimates currently published in ARTS, AWTS, SAS, ASM, and ACES 
will be produced as part of the AIES and expanded to include 
subnational data across the economy. Previously, the ASM 
(manufacturing) was the only annual survey being integrated into the 
AIES that produced subnational data. The AIES will produce subnational 
data for manufacturing, retail, wholesale, and service sectors if 
quality standards are met. The AIES information previously collected on 
the Report of Organization will continue to be used to update the 
Census Bureau's BR, and the AIES data previously collected on the M3UFO 
will continue to be used for the Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, 
and Orders (M3) Survey benchmarking purposes. Data users will be able 
to access the AIES estimates through the use of visualizations, CSV 
files, data.census.gov, and the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED), 
which is an online database maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of 
St. Louis.
    Private businesses, organizations, industry analysts, educators and 
students, and economic researchers have used the data and estimates 
provided by the ARTS, AWTS, SAS, ASM, and ACES collections for 
analyzing and conducting impact evaluations on past and current 
economic performance, short-term economic forecasts, productivity, 
long-term economic growth, market analysis, tax policy, capacity 
utilization, business fixed capital stocks and capital formation, 
domestic and international competitiveness trade policy, product 
development, market research, and financial analysis. Trade and 
professional organizations have used the estimates to analyze industry 
trends and benchmark their own statistical programs, develop forecasts, 
and evaluate regulatory requirements. Government program officials and 
agencies have used the data for research, economic policy making, and 
forecasting.
    Based on the use of the data of the existing collections, estimates 
produced from the AIES will serve as a benchmark for Census Bureau 
indicator programs, such as the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and 
Food Services (MARTS), the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS), 
Manufacturers' Shipments Inventories & Orders (M3), Monthly Wholesale 
Trade Survey (MWTS), and the Quarterly Services Survey (QSS). Like the 
previous collections, the AIES will provide updates to the Longitudinal 
Research Database (LRD), and Census Bureau staff and academic 
researchers with special sworn status will continue to use the LRD for 
micro data analysis. The Census Bureau will also continue to use 
information collected in the AIES to update and maintain the 
centralized, multipurpose BR that provides sampling populations and 
enumeration lists for the Census Bureau's economic surveys and 
censuses.
    The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) will continue to use the 
estimates to derive industry output for the input-output accounts and 
for the gross domestic product (GDP). The Bureau of Labor Statistics 
(BLS) will continue to use the data as input to its Producer Price 
Index (PPI) and in developing productivity measurements; the Federal 
Reserve Board (FRB) will continue to use the data to prepare the Index 
of Industrial Production, to improve estimates of investment indicators 
for monetary policy, and in monitoring retail credit lending; the 
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) will continue to use 
the data to estimate expenditures for the National Health Accounts and 
for monitoring and evaluating healthcare industries; and the Department 
of the Treasury will continue to use the data to analyze depreciation 
and to research economic trends.
    Frequency: Annually.
    Respondent's Obligation: Mandatory.
    Legal Authority: The AIES collection is authorized by title 13 
U.S.C. 131, 182, and 193. Response to the AIES is mandatory per 
sections 224 and 225 of title 13 U.S.C.
    This information collection request may be viewed at 
www.reginfo.gov. Follow the instructions to view the Department of 
Commerce collections currently under review by OMB.
    Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information 
collection should be submitted within 30 days of the publication of 
this notice on the following website www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain. 
Find this particular information collection by selecting ``Currently 
under 30-day Review--Open for Public Comments'' or by using the search 
function and entering the title of the collection.

Department PRA Clearance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for 
Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau

September 2, 2025 – March 19, 2026 IF13105

Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau
Updated March 19, 2026 (IF13105)

Introduction

As a Department of Commerce agency, the U.S. Census Bureau is primarily funded through the annual Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS) appropriations bill. This In Focus provides an overview of FY2026 appropriations for the U.S. Census Bureau; certain comparisons to previous years' appropriations; and congressional action to date. Information presented is drawn from the Census Bureau's FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification, the enacted FY2026 CJS bill, and other relevant congressional documents.

The FY2026 appropriations are divided between two accounts: Current Surveys and Programs, and Periodic Censuses and Programs. For these two accounts, comparisons are made here between the FY2026 enacted level, the FY2026 request, and enacted amounts for FY2024 and FY2025. (The FY2025 full-year continuing resolution [CR] funded these accounts in the same amounts and under the same authorities and conditions as enacted in FY2024.) The FY2026 budget justification also includes requested amounts below the account level in more detail, which are compared here to corresponding actual FY2024 amounts (the budget justification document does not provide this level of detail for FY2025 actual amounts).

Figure 1. Census Budget Authority

Source: Data from U.S. Census Bureau, FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification and FY2026 Appropriations.

Notes: Values may not add evenly due to rounding.

FY2026 Appropriations

The enacted FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74) includes $1.490 billion for the Census Bureau. This is $186 million less than the Trump Administration's FY2026 budget request of $1.677 billion and a $108 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted levels of $1.383 billion.

Current Surveys and Programs

The bill includes $319 million for the Current Surveys and Programs account, which is $30 million above the Administration's FY2026 requested $289 million and a decrease of $10 million from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amounts of $329 million. This account includes funding for Current Economic Statistics and Current Demographic Statistics.

Current Economic Statistics

Current Economic Statistics include business, construction, manufacturing, general economic, foreign trade, and government statistics. According to the FY2026 budget justification, Current Economic Statistics programs "provide timely, accurate, and essential data on the structure and performance of the U.S. economy, supporting the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) estimation, fiscal and monetary policymaking, and private sector decision-making."

The FY2026 request for Current Economic Statistics was $216 million, the same as FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts.

Current Demographic Statistics

Current Demographic Statistics includes the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP); the Current Population Survey (CPS), which is sponsored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the Census Bureau; and the Population Estimates Program. The SIPP is an ongoing survey that measures distribution of government assistance programs. The CPS provides estimates of income, poverty, and other indicators. The Population Estimates Program calculates population change over time. The Census Bureau's population estimates are used in a variety of federal programs to determine funding allocations or eligibility.

The FY2026 request for Current Demographic Statistics was $73 million, which is a $40 million decrease from FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts of $113 million.

Proposed changes to these programs include testing internet self-response for the CPS and using some nonsurvey data to reduce costs for the SIPP.

Periodic Censuses and Programs

The bill includes $1.172 billion for the Periodic Censuses and Programs account, which is $216 million less than the Administration's FY2026 requested $1.388 billion and a $118 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amount of $1.054 billion. This account consists of funding for several programs discussed below.

Decennial Census

The FY2026 request for the decennial census account was $983 million, a $383 million increase from the FY2024 actual amount of $600 million. Requested FY2026 funding for the decennial census includes support for the 2026 Census Test and preparation for the 2028 Dress Rehearsal, full-scale development of core IT infrastructure, award and management of contracts, and continued data collection and publication for the American Community Survey (ACS). Unlike previous budget documents, the FY2026 budget justification does not specify the respective amounts for the 2030 decennial census and the ACS within the decennial census account.

Periodic Economic Statistics

The FY2026 request for the Periodic Economic Statistics Program, which contains the Economic Census and the Census of Governments, was $144 million, an $18 million decrease from the FY2024 actual level of $162 million. Specific funding levels for these two surveys are not provided in the FY2026 budget request.

The Economic Census, conducted every five years, collects statistics on businesses in the United States to help understand the U.S. economy. Requested FY2026 activities for the Economic Census include the continued review of 2022 Economic Census data releases.

The Census of Governments, conducted every five years, collects statistics on state and local governments across the United States. Requested FY2026 activities for the Census of Governments include the expanded use of administrative records and other data collection methods in preparation for the 2027 Census of Governments.

Geographic Support Program

The purpose of the Census Bureau's Geographic Support Program (GSP) is to support and maintain the geospatial infrastructure required to conduct survey data collection, processing, tabulation, and dissemination across covered regions. The Census Bureau considers the GSP to be foundational for all of its social and economic data products. Congressional district wall maps are produced by the GSP. The Census Bureau aims to utilize the GSP to minimize 2030 Census in-field enumeration costs.

The FY2026 request for the GSP was $98 million, a $14 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $112 million.

Enterprise Data Collection and Dissemination Systems (EDCaDS)

The EDCaDS generally supports the data collection, processing, and dissemination systems that are associated with Census Bureau programs.

The FY2026 request's stated goal for the EDCaDS is "to provide large cyclical systems that must be scaled for peak operations for the Decennial Census, the Economic Census, and the Census of Governments."

The FY2026 request for the EDCaDS was $163 million, a $17 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $180 million.

Congressional Action

The House Appropriations Committee CJS subcommittee marked up the House version of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 15, 2025. The bill, as approved by the subcommittee, would have provided $1.677 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $288.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.388 billion for Periodic Censuses and Programs. The bill, as reported, would have prohibited the Census Bureau from using any funds provided in the measure to include "aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States" in rendering apportionment determinations. It also included similar prohibitions on using any funds provided to enforce mandatory response requirements for certain Census Bureau surveys or to inquire more than twice to solicit voluntary survey responses. These provisions were not included in the version of the bill subsequently enacted into law. The bill advanced from the subcommittee by a 9-6 vote. The full committee ordered the bill reported by a 34-28 vote on September 10, 2025.

The Senate Appropriations Committee marked up its FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 17, 2025. The bill, as reported, would have provided $1.520 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $328.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.192 billion for Periodic Census and Programs. Furthermore, the committee report accompanying the bill directs the Census Bureau to provide information regarding the removal of Census and BEA data sets; the termination of Census Bureau advisory committees; ACS modernization efforts; 2030 decennial census operation plans; and the effects of field office closures. The report directs the Census Bureau to continue outreach to public libraries as partners for surveys and to prioritize carrying out the 2026 Census Test. The committee ordered the bill reported by a 19-10 vote.

Census Bureau appropriations lapsed from October 1 through November 12, 2025. The lapse ended when a CR providing appropriations for certain agencies (including the Commerce Department) through January 30, 2026, became law. The FY2026 CJS appropriations bill was included as part of a consolidated appropriations measure, which passed the House by a vote of 397-28 on January 8, 2026, and passed the Senate by a vote of 82-15 on January 15, 2026. The bill was signed into law by President Trump on January 23, 2026. The explanatory statement for the FY2026 CJS bill was filed in the Congressional Record by the chair of the House Appropriations Committee on January 8, 2026. The explanatory statement specifies that the Appropriations Committee reports accompanying the House and Senate versions of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill carry "the same weight as language included in this joint explanatory statement and should be complied with unless specifically addressed to the contrary in this joint explanatory statement or in the act."

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES)
Description: The Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES) replaced and integrated seven annual business surveys (Annual Retail Trade Survey, Annual Wholesale Survey, Service Annual Survey, Annual Survey of Manufactures, Annual Capital Expenditures Survey, Manufacturer's Unfilled Orders Survey , Report of Organization) into one survey. The AIES provides the most comprehensive national and subnational data on business revenues, expenses, payroll, and employment on an annual basis.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES): research and preservation report

**Research checked:** October 8, 2026  
**Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce  
**Status:** Active annual statistical program; public data available for reference years **2023 and 2024**.

## Executive findings

Your description is **substantially accurate** and closely matches the Census Bureau’s description. AIES replaced and integrated seven annual business surveys. It produces annual statistics on business revenue, expenses, payroll, employment, inventories, and other economic measures, with more geographic detail than many predecessor programs offered.

Five qualifications are essential:

1. **AIES is a program and a family of datasets—not one file.** Its public products include summary tables, sector-specific tables, APIs, downloadable files, visualizations, and experimental estimates.
2. **The core survey covers employer businesses.** It is not a census of every business, sole proprietor, government operation, or agricultural producer.
3. **Coverage is uneven across industries and variables.** Some industries receive only a limited set of questions; not every collected item becomes a public estimate.
4. **“Subnational” does not mean county- or neighborhood-level coverage.** The main releases provide national, regional, divisional, and selected state estimates. Geographic availability depends on the table and industry.
5. **The transition creates important comparability issues.** Census links many estimates to predecessor series, but some expense and other series are not comparable across the transition.

**Preservation priority:** High. AIES now carries forward much of the annual statistical infrastructure previously distributed across seven programs. Preserving its data without its methodology, classifications, flags, historical releases, and predecessor documentation would preserve numbers but lose much of their meaning.

Sources: [AIES program overview](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies.html), [2023 main-release announcement](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/main-release-of-aies-data.html), and [2024 release announcement](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2024-aies-data-release.html).

---

## 1. Dataset identity and recommended catalog description

| Element | Verified information |
|---|---|
| Official title | Annual Integrated Economic Survey |
| Acronym | AIES |
| Responsible agency | U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce |
| Program area | Census Bureau economic statistics |
| Frequency | Annual |
| First production reference year | 2023, collected beginning in calendar year 2024 |
| Earlier testing | Pilots and a reference-year-2022 dress rehearsal |
| Public reference years located | 2023 and 2024 |
| Core population | Domestic private-sector, nonfarm employer businesses, subject to industry-specific coverage rules |
| Geographic universe | Fifty states and the District of Columbia |
| Classification | Published 2023 and 2024 releases use **2017 NAICS** |
| Sampling/reporting unit | Company or firm; collection also uses establishment and other within-company detail |
| Public data type | Aggregate statistical estimates, not identifiable company records |
| Principal access routes | data.census.gov, Census bulk-download directory, Census Data API; selected series through FRED |
| OMB control number | **0607-1024** |

### Suggested replacement for the supplied description

> The Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES), published annually by the U.S. Census Bureau, integrates and replaces seven predecessor annual business surveys beginning with reference year 2023. It provides aggregate estimates of revenue, expenses, payroll, employment, inventories, and selected additional measures for domestic employer businesses. Products include national, regional, divisional, and selected state estimates, with industry, variable, and geographic coverage varying by table. The survey combines business responses, administrative records, imputation, weighting, and links to predecessor estimates and the Economic Census.

This is more precise than describing AIES as uniformly comprehensive across all businesses and geographies.

---

## 2. Who publishes it, and under what authority?

### Institutional responsibility

The **Census Bureau** collects, processes, protects, and publishes AIES. The **Department of Commerce** is its parent department. Other federal agencies use the results, but they are not the primary publishers.

### Legal authority and mandatory response

Census identifies:

- **13 U.S.C. §§ 131 and 182** as authority for the collection.
- **13 U.S.C. §§ 224 and 225** as the provisions requiring response and addressing noncompliance.
- **13 U.S.C. § 9** as the requirement to protect confidential responses and use them for statistical purposes.

The 2023 implementation notice also cited **§ 193**, including in connection with using dress-rehearsal information to supplement Economic Census responses.

AIES is therefore **mandatory for selected businesses**, not a voluntary opinion survey. Census’s FAQ explains possible penalties but emphasizes cooperative collection rather than prosecution.

Sources: [About AIES](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies/about.html), [AIES FAQ](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies/faq.html), and [April 4, 2023 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-04-04/html/2023-06947.htm).

### OMB approval and public oversight

The survey is approved under the **Paperwork Reduction Act** process, with OMB control number **0607-1024**. That process provides opportunities to comment on necessity, utility, burden, and collection design.

An important distinction: the cited statutes authorize economic statistics and compel selected respondents to answer; the reviewed materials do **not** establish that Congress enacted a separate law specifically requiring a survey named “AIES” or guaranteeing every particular AIES table.

### Funding

AIES is a federal Census Bureau program. I did not establish a separate, current AIES-only appropriation or independently audited program cost from the reviewed sources. **Respondent burden estimates are not the program’s operating budget.**

---

## 3. History: why it exists and what it replaced

### Rationale for integration

AIES responds to longstanding problems with separately administered annual economic surveys:

- Multiple requests to the same company.
- Differences in concepts, collection units, questionnaires, and processing.
- Difficulty analyzing companies operating across industries.
- Inconsistent geographic detail.
- Opportunities to reduce duplication and standardize operations.

The objectives were to **reduce respondent burden, improve data coherence and quality, and lower long-term operating costs**. These are program goals, not proof that every benefit has already been achieved.

### Development timeline

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 2015–2018 | National Academies review of Census annual economic surveys; final report, *Reengineering the Census Bureau’s Annual Economic Surveys*, issued in 2018 |
| 2019–2020 | Coordinated-collection research involving services, retail, and wholesale surveys |
| 2021 | Recordkeeping and accessibility studies; pilot involving 78 companies and 2,863 establishments |
| 2022 | Further cognitive testing and instrument development; public proposal for AIES |
| 2023 | Dress rehearsal collecting reference-year-2022 information |
| 2024 | Full production collection begins for reference year 2023 |
| July 2025 | Preliminary 2023 “First Look” estimates released |
| February 26, 2026 | Main 2023 release; final estimates supersede the preliminary First Look estimates |
| April 30, 2026 | Initial experimental capital-expenditures release |
| September 3, 2026 | Full 2024 dataset released |

Sources: [National Academies study](https://www.nationalacademies.org/projects/DBASSE-CNSTAT-15-06), [November 4, 2022 proposal](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/11/04/2022-24035/annual-integrated-economic-survey), [2023 implementation notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-04-04/html/2023-06947.htm), and release announcements linked above.

### The seven predecessor surveys

| Predecessor | Principal function carried into AIES |
|---|---|
| Annual Retail Trade Survey — ARTS | Retail sales, expenses, inventories, and related measures |
| Annual Wholesale Trade Survey — AWTS | Wholesale sales, inventories, purchases, and expenses |
| Service Annual Survey — SAS | Service-industry revenue, expenses, and specialized measures |
| Annual Survey of Manufactures — ASM | Manufacturing shipments, employment, payroll, costs, inventories, and other production statistics |
| Annual Capital Expenditures Survey — ACES | Investment in structures and equipment |
| Manufacturers’ Unfilled Orders Survey — M3UFO | Information supporting manufacturing unfilled-orders statistics and benchmarking |
| Report of Organization | Company structure and organizational information used to maintain the Business Register |

The supplied name **“Annual Wholesale Survey”** should be **“Annual Wholesale Trade Survey.”** “Service Annual Survey” is the established SAS title, although some Census metadata uses “Services Annual Survey.”

The 2023 notice specified that ASM and the Report of Organization had their last standalone survey year in **2021**, while ACES, ARTS, AWTS, SAS, and M3UFO had their last standalone survey year in **2022**. Consequently, **2022 is not simply a missing AIES year**; understanding it requires the Economic Census, legacy products, and transition documentation.

Integration also does not mean all seven predecessors map one-to-one to seven public AIES tables. Some information primarily supports internal statistical infrastructure or other programs.

---

## 4. What population does AIES actually describe?

### Core scope

The headline universe is businesses that:

- Operated during at least some part of the reference year.
- Had paid employees.
- Operated domestically in the fifty states or D.C.
- Fell within covered private-sector industries.

It excludes foreign operations of U.S. companies, most government entities, agricultural production companies, private households, and businesses in U.S. territories.

**Private-sector does not mean exclusively for-profit:** covered tax-exempt organizations are included in relevant industries.

### Industry coverage is not uniform

The production methodology distinguishes broad coverage from limited and supplemental collection.

Broadly covered sectors include utilities; manufacturing; wholesale and retail trade; transportation and warehousing; information; finance and insurance; real estate; professional and technical services; administrative and waste-management services; education; health care; arts and recreation; accommodation and food services; and other services.

However, the methodology lists important exceptions within these sectors. It also identifies limited-scope collection for:

- Support activities for agriculture and forestry.
- Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction.
- Construction.
- Management of companies and enterprises.
- Labor unions and similar organizations.
- Political organizations.

Other excluded or specially treated industries include agricultural production, postal service, certain financial vehicles, rail transportation, specified educational institutions, religious organizations, and private households.

**Do not infer publication coverage merely because an industry was asked questions or appears in an API classification list.** A multi-industry company may report limited information for activities outside the main publication universe.

Source: [2023 AIES methodology](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies/technical-documentation/methodology/2023-aies-methodology.pdf).

### Nonemployer businesses: an important exception to the exception

The core survey does **not** sample businesses without paid employees. But a separate **AIES–Nonemployer Statistics** product combines employer revenue estimates with administrative-record-based Nonemployer Statistics for comparable industries.

For 2023:

- AIES used **2017 NAICS**.
- Nonemployer Statistics used **2022 NAICS**.
- Census converted relevant nonemployer records to a 2017 basis for the combined table.

That combined table is a **linked statistical product**, not evidence that nonemployers answered the AIES questionnaire.

Source: [2023 AIES–NES methodology](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies/technical-documentation/methodology/2023-aies-nes-methodology.pdf).

---

## 5. What information is collected and published?

### Common measures

Important public variables include:

- Sales, value of shipments, or revenue.
- Annual payroll.
- First-quarter payroll.
- Employment.
- Operating expenses.
- Inventories.
- E-commerce activity.
- Capital expenditures, currently including experimental products.

### Sector-specific detail

Products also include:

- **Manufacturing:** value added, production-worker wages and hours, fuels, electricity, materials, contract work, and inventory components.
- **Wholesale and retail:** purchases, gross margins, inventory valuation, and selected e-commerce detail.
- **Services:** revenue by product or class of customer and detailed expenses.
- **Health care:** telemedicine revenue, inpatient days, outpatient visits, patient visits, revenue by payer, and electronic-health-record expenses.

The collection also includes company characteristics, ownership and organizational changes, business classifications, and robotics information. **Collection content should not be treated as a list of publicly available variables.**

Sources: [2023 collection notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-04-04/html/2023-06947.htm), [2023 tables](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2023/econ/aies/2023-aies-tables.html), and [2024 tables](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2024/econ/aies/2024-aies-tables.html).

### Units and interpretation

Selected 2024 API fields illustrate the structure:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `RCPT_TOT_VAL` | Sales, value of shipments, or revenue, **$1,000** |
| `PAY_ANN_VAL` | Annual payroll, **$1,000** |
| `PAY_QTR1_VAL` | First-quarter payroll, **$1,000** |
| `EMP_MAR12_NUM` | Number of employees |
| `EXPS_TOT_DVAL` | Operating expenses, **$1,000** |
| `RCPT_TOT_CV` | Revenue coefficient of variation, percent |
| `NAICS2017` | Industry code |
| `TAXSTAT` | Tax-status category |
| `TYPOP` | Type-of-operation category |

Preserve the corresponding `_F` flags, labels, and footnotes.

Two interpretation cautions:

- The main dollar estimates are **not adjusted for price changes**.
- The employment field identifies a **March 12 employment measure**, not an annual-average workforce. Dividing annual payroll by it does not produce a worker-level wage distribution.

“Revenue” also has sector-specific meaning: retail sales, manufacturing shipments, and service receipts are not interchangeable accounting concepts.

## 7. How the estimates are produced

The following details are documented for the **2023 methodology**. Analysts should use the corresponding methodology for each later release rather than assume it is unchanged.

### Sampling frame and design

- The frame comes from the Census **Business Register**.
- It combines establishment information into company-level sampling units.
- The initial frame uses December 2023 Business Register information and additional 2022 Economic Census information.
- Approximately **385,000 companies** are sampled.
- Approximately **48,500 companies** are identified as certainty units.
- Administrative annual payroll is the principal measure of size.
- Stratification incorporates industry and geography, and selected sectors also use tax status or type of operation.
- Selection uses unequal-probability, without-replacement **Chromy sampling**.

This is a probability sample, **not a simple random sample** and not a full census of businesses.

### Collection

Businesses receive reporting instructions and use an electronic instrument, including spreadsheet-based reporting. Census follows up through mail, email, and telephone.

Within-company reporting detail depends on the item and industry. For example, capital expenditures are collected at the establishment level for manufacturing and at a **Kind of Activity Unit** level for other sectors, with a company total also requested.

### Nonresponse and imputation

Missing or unusable items are imputed using methods including:

- Regression.
- Substitution.
- Nearest-neighbor hot deck.

Published totals combine reported, administrative-record, and imputed information.

### Estimation

Totals use a **Horvitz–Thompson estimator**: weighted reported and imputed values are summed, with a sampling weight based on the reciprocal of selection probability. Linking and benchmarking adjustments also affect published series.

Sources: [2023 methodology](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies/technical-documentation/methodology/2023-aies-methodology.pdf), [2024 methodology](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies/technical-documentation/methodology/2024-aies-methodology-final.pdf), and [capital-expenditures technical documentation](https://www2.census.gov/data/experimental-data-products/capex-aies/capex-technical-documentation.pdf).

## 8. Quality, uncertainty, and confidentiality

### Response rates

The 2023 methodology reports:

- **Overall unit response rate: 64.2%.**
- **Revenue total-quantity response rate: 60% to less than 70%.**

These are different measures:

- The unit rate measures responding units.
- The total-quantity rate measures the weighted proportion of an item’s estimate supplied by responses or equivalent-quality sources.

Nonresponse does not mean nonresponding businesses are simply omitted. Their values can be supplied through administrative records or imputation. Neither does a large sample eliminate nonresponse bias.

### Sampling and nonsampling error

AIES provides coefficients of variation and related quality flags. Analysts should account for:

- Sampling variability.
- Frame undercoverage or misclassification.
- Reporting and interpretation errors.
- Item and unit nonresponse.
- Imputation assumptions.
- Processing errors.
- Changes in questionnaire content and collection design.

For a positive estimate, an approximate standard error can be calculated as:

\[
SE \approx \text{estimate}\times CV/100
\]

But comparing years, geographies, or related estimates can require covariance information or Census-provided trend errors. Do not automatically assume independence.

### Suppression and flags

The 2023 core methodology uses **cell suppression**:

- Primary suppression protects confidential values.
- Complementary suppression prevents disclosure through subtraction.
- Suppressed data remain included in higher-level totals.

Important symbols include:

- `D`: withheld to protect individual-company information.
- `S`: does not meet publication standards.
- `Z`: rounds to zero.
- `v` and `w`: high-variability warnings under the documented thresholds.

A suppressed cell is **not zero**, and a complementary suppression is not evidence that a cell is intrinsically sensitive or unusually small.

The combined employer/nonemployer product uses two protection systems: **AIES suppression** and **NES noise infusion**. Preserve their separate indicators.

### Restricted microdata

The public releases do not provide identifiable firm-level data. Census’s restricted-use inventory lists AIES reference year **2023** as firm microdata. Access is through approved research arrangements at secure **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers**, with authorization for specific datasets.

Public 2024 tables do not establish that restricted-use 2024 microdata are already available.

Source: [Census restricted-use economic data inventory](https://www.census.gov/topics/research/guidance/restricted-use-microdata/economic-data.html).

## 9. Comparability with predecessor surveys and across releases

This is one of the most consequential issues for research and preservation.

### Linking to legacy series

For most industries, Census calculates a **carry-forward factor** using:

- Numerator: final, census-adjusted 2022 legacy revenue estimate.
- Denominator: 2022 revenue estimate from the new AIES sample.

It applies that ratio to AIES estimates to link the series. For many industries, this also links estimates indirectly to the **2022 Economic Census**.

The methodology notes that legacy estimates must first be converted from **millions to thousands of dollars**.

### Important breaks

The 2023 methodology states:

- Outside manufacturing, **total and detailed expenses are not linked to legacy expense estimates because of scope differences**.
- Selected revenue-detail series, such as certain newspaper-publishing measures, begin new series because questionnaires changed.
- Certain industries use direct Economic Census-based factors rather than the usual legacy-survey linkage.

The current Census visualization also says operating-expense trends are not provided because of collection changes.

**Practical rule:** Do not append AIES to an older survey and calculate growth until you have checked the item-level linking rules.

### Preliminary, final, and later versions

The February 2026 main release explicitly superseded July 2025 First Look estimates. However, “final” does not mean “immutable forever.”

The live 2023 download directory contains both current files and a [`SY23_ARCHIVE`](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/aies/data/2023/SY23_ARCHIVE/) directory. Current files also have modification dates later than the initial main release. File timestamps alone do not establish what changed, but they make release-specific preservation essential.

### Benefits to the public

1. **Free access to detailed economic evidence** that many small organizations could not otherwise purchase.
2. **Better annual geographic information**, particularly for sectors whose predecessors mainly published national estimates.
3. **A stronger foundation for widely used indicators**, including national accounts and productivity measures.
4. **More consistent cross-industry analysis**, especially for firms spanning multiple sectors.
5. **Potentially less duplicate reporting** for businesses.
6. **Greater policy accountability**, through independent analysis of regional, sectoral, health-care, investment, and digital-commerce trends.

### What it cannot establish by itself

AIES is not sufficient on its own to measure:

- Individual wages, working conditions, or discrimination.
- Racial or gender disparities in business ownership.
- Corporate political influence.
- Neighborhood economic conditions.
- Market concentration from public aggregate tables alone.
- Causal effects of a policy.
- GDP by simply summing industry revenue.

Revenue includes intermediate transactions; it is not the same as value added. Policy analyses often need AIES alongside demographic, labor, ownership, price, and other economic datasets.

## 12. Data-science recommendations

1. **Keep a raw-data layer.** Preserve original downloads and API responses before cleaning.
2. **Preserve codes as strings.** NAICS, FIPS, and geography identifiers should not be converted indiscriminately to numbers.
3. **Retain all dimensions.** Year, geography, industry, tax status, type of operation, and specialized categories may be needed to uniquely identify rows.
4. **Avoid double counting.** Do not sum national and regional rows, parent and child NAICS categories, or total and component categories.
5. **Keep values, CVs, and flags together.** Never turn all nonnumeric or sentinel values into zero.
6. **Document dollar units.** AIES commonly publishes thousands of dollars; predecessor tables may use millions.
7. **Use matching classifications.** Do not join 2017 and 2022 NAICS by code alone.
8. **Distinguish direct and experimental estimates.** Model-based state estimates and product projections require separate provenance.
9. **Use appropriate deflators** for real growth and document the choice.
10. **Treat public rows as aggregates, not firms.** Firm-level prediction, concentration, and behavioral analysis require suitable microdata.
11. **Version analytical outputs.** Record which preliminary, main, or later file release produced each result.
12. **Validate against official totals and table notes**, allowing for rounding and suppressed cells.

### Recommended archival practices

These are preservation recommendations, not documented Census requirements:

- Create immutable snapshots for each release.
- Preserve original ZIP/PDF/JSON files and open-format derivatives.
- Record source URLs, acquisition timestamps, release dates, file sizes, and **SHA-256 checksums**.
- Maintain a manifest associating data with its documentation.
- Capture directory listings and relevant web pages.
- Compare later downloads against earlier checksums and schemas.
- Keep at least two independently managed copies.
- Preserve API query text but remove private API keys.
- Record whether each product is preliminary, standard, experimental, revised, or superseded.

The inspected 2023 directory’s compressed table files are relatively small, making complete public-table preservation feasible for a modest repository. That does not include restricted microdata or all historical documentation.

### Principal risks

- Live URLs can continue to exist while files change.
- Documentation can be updated without a distinct versioned URL.
- API authentication and schemas can change.
- Experimental products may change methodology or cease.
- Legacy websites may become harder to navigate after integration.
- Budget or staffing changes can affect timeliness and detail.

The presence of a Census archive directory is useful, but it is not a verified guarantee of permanent retention of every version.

## Bottom line

**AIES is a major replacement and modernization of federal annual business statistics.** Your description is correct at the program level, but it needs explicit qualifications about employer coverage, industry exceptions, geographic availability, experimental products, uncertainty, and time-series breaks.

For a librarian or preservationist, the right preservation target is **the complete versioned statistical package**—data, metadata, methodology, collection instruments, legal history, and predecessor links. **Prioritize preservation now**, especially because losses of future measurement cannot be repaired by archiving later releases.

1. Preserve 2023 and 2024 bulk files, First Look files, and the complete `SY23_ARCHIVE`.
2. Save questionnaires, change summaries, methodology, flags, API schemas, and NAICS/NAPCS documentation.
3. Capture the 2025–2026 ICR packages and content-change attachments.
4. Record acquisition dates and checksums; distinguish preliminary, revised, and archived releases.
5. Monitor future publication dates, public-variable availability, suppression rates, and detailed-content frequency.
